contents:
A Forge app works perfectly when you test it as a Jira administrator. You switch to an ordinary project member, try the same action, and get a permission error. It can be tempting to change the API call from asUser() to asApp() and move on.
Before doing that, check whether the error is the correct result. If the user isn’t allowed to edit the issue, making the request succeed with the app’s permissions may introduce the very problem the platform was preventing.
Follow one operation all the way through Take an app that lets a project manager update an issue’s reporting classification. The browser sends an issue ID and the new classification to a resolver. The resolver calls Jira.
There are two permission decisions here. Jira controls whether the caller can edit that issue. Your app may impose an additional rule: perhaps only the reporting owner should be able to change the classification. Passing the first check doesn’t satisfy the second.
Write those decisions down before choosing the API context. It makes the code review much easier: a reviewer can see why the app needs a particular permission and where that permission is checked.
Start with the user’s permissions Atlassian’s shared responsibility model says to use asUser() for an operation performed on a user’s behalf. Before an asApp() call, the app must verify the expected permissions. The platform handles parts of authentication; the developer still owns the application’s authorisation logic.
For the classification example, ask whether the action should succeed when the current user cannot edit the issue in Jira. Usually, it shouldn’t. That gives you a useful starting point for both implementation and testing.
App-context calls have legitimate uses, including background work. The important part is having a reason for the additional authority and a check that limits its use. “The other call returned 403” is a debugging observation, not that reason.
The Forge Authorize API provides helpers for checking user permissions before app-context requests. Choose the check for the actual operation and resource. Handle a failed check without making the change, and handle a later API refusal too: permissions can change between requests.
Test with someone who cannot do the job An administrator account is convenient during development, but it hides permission mistakes. For this example, use at least these cases:
Account Attempt Expected result Permitted project member Update an allowed issue Change succeeds Read-only member Update that same issue Change is rejected Member of a different project Submit a restricted issue ID Access is denied User whose access was just removed Repeat a previously allowed change The next change is denied Check the stored issue after each rejected request. An error response doesn’t help if the resolver changed the data before returning it.
Also change the issue ID sent by the browser. Hiding an option in the UI won’t stop a caller from submitting a different value. The resolver needs to validate the input and make its own permission decision. Atlassian’s resolver reference explains the context available to backend functions; use it carefully rather than trusting identity or permission claims in the payload.
Leave the next developer a useful explanation Near each privileged operation, make the intent clear: which user or job initiated it, which resource it affects, and why app authority is needed. A short comment explaining that decision is more useful than one that merely repeats the API method name.
When a permission test fails, keep it as a regression case. It’s easy for a later refactor to preserve the successful workflow while accidentally removing the check that protected it.
References Forge shared responsibility model Forge Authorize API Forge resolver reference Reviewed 10 November 2026. The classification app is a worked example.
title: Checking permissions in Forge: when to use asUser and asApp

contents:
Suppose two customers use your reporting app. Both have a report numbered 42. The database keeps their records separate, but the remote backend caches a generated report under the key report:42.
The database design is fine. The cache has lost the customer boundary.
This is the sort of detail worth looking for when a Forge app starts using a remote backend. Reviewing only the incoming HTTP handler leaves a lot of the data path unchecked.
Begin at the incoming request The backend needs to establish that a request came from Forge and is intended for your app. Atlassian requires verification of the Forge Invocation Token (FIT), including its signature and expected audience, using the appropriate signing keys. The expected app ID must come from trusted configuration. Forge Remote essentials describes that contract.
Decoding a JWT only makes its claims readable. It doesn’t verify them. Don’t use an unverified claim or a tenantId field in the request body to decide which customer’s records to open.
Use a maintained verification library and check the current guidance for the environment you’re deploying into. Keep access tokens out of logs, including error logs. A debugging statement that prints an entire request can undo otherwise careful credential handling.
Follow the customer identifier into storage Once the request has been verified, follow the trusted installation context through every place data is stored or retrieved. For the report example, review the database lookup, cache key, export filename, download permission, and background job payload.
A useful review exercise is to put the two customer requests side by side. At each step, identify what prevents customer A’s request from selecting customer B’s report. If the answer depends on a convention that isn’t enforced in code, investigate it.
Atlassian recommends associating remotely stored data with installationId. Its documentation also explains that this identifier changes on reinstallation. Decide how your service handles that transition. An assertion from a newly installed client should not be enough to reconnect old customer data.
Include the paths people forget to draw Architecture diagrams often show the normal request and response, then stop. Add the other paths before the review:
A queued export that runs after the user has left the page. A retry after the backend timed out. A support tool used to inspect a failed job. A cached download that remains available after permissions change. These are not necessarily vulnerabilities. They are places where the identity, timing, or permission decision may differ from the interactive request. Make that difference explicit.
Check the payload as well as the destination The Forge permissions manifest declares scopes and access to external resources. Keep those declarations narrow and consistent with the application’s needs.
Then inspect what the app actually sends. A service that summarises one selected paragraph may not need the entire issue history. Check ordinary requests, retries, and failure logs; the latter two can contain more data than the successful path.
Agree where that data is retained and how it is deleted. This is easier to answer while designing the integration than after several services have each kept their own copy.
A small release check In an authorised test environment, use synthetic records for two installations. Try a missing token, an invalid token, an unexpected app identity, and a request for the other installation’s report. Confirm that the request is rejected before data is returned or changed.
Repeat a completed export request and inspect the result. Depending on the workflow, it may return an existing export or create another one; either way, the behaviour should be deliberate and remain within the correct customer boundary.
Keep these checks alongside the functional integration tests. A successful report download proves the feature works. These cases establish who can obtain it.
References Forge Remote essentials Forge manifest permissions Security requirements for cloud apps Reviewed 10 November 2026. The reporting service is a worked example.
title: What to check before putting a Forge Remote backend into production

contents:
“We need an OWASP test before launch.” It’s a reasonable request, but the next conversation needs to be about the application: which users it serves, what they can do, and what would go wrong if a control failed.
A customer portal with invoice downloads needs different attention from a public content site. Both are web applications. Giving each the same checklist can leave important behaviour unexplored.
Which OWASP reference do you mean? Several OWASP resources are useful here, and they do different jobs.
The Top 10:2025 describes major web application risk categories. It gives teams a common vocabulary, but it isn’t an exhaustive testing scope.
The Web Security Testing Guide v4.2 describes testing techniques. ASVS 5.0.0 provides security requirements that can inform development and verification. The API Security Top 10:2023 adds an API perspective, including object-level and function-level authorisation risks.
An assessment can draw on several of these. Its scope should identify which versions and which applicable controls or tests it uses. “Latest OWASP” won’t tell a future reader what was assessed.
Work through a feature the business cares about Take a portal that lets a customer export invoices. Start with the intended behaviour: a customer should be able to download invoices belonging to their own account, and an employee’s access should follow their role.
Now turn that into test questions. Can the customer request an invoice belonging to someone else? Can a read-only employee start an export? What happens to an existing download link after access is removed? Does a queued export use the same customer boundary as the request that created it?
Those questions also tell you what preparation is needed. You need more than one account, suitable roles, sample invoices, and access to the relevant export workflow. Without them, parts of the assessment may remain unverified.
Keep a record of coverage, including the gaps A short coverage record can be more informative than a long list of scanner results:
Area What the record should show Invoice ownership The account used, the requested invoice, and the observed response Export permissions The user’s role and whether an export was created Revoked access The permission change and the behaviour afterwards Queued exports The job’s identity and the customer context used during processing Record exclusions and checks that couldn’t be completed. A feature that was not tested should never look the same as a feature that was tested without a finding. This matters when someone uses the report to decide whether a release can proceed.
Write for the engineer who will fix it “Broken access control” is a category, not enough information to repair a defect. A useful finding identifies the endpoint or workflow, the access needed to reproduce it, the steps taken, and the result. It then explains the impact supported by that evidence.
For the invoice example, say which ownership check was missing and where it needs to be enforced. Include a test the developer can run after the change. If a wider impact is plausible but wasn’t verified, say so rather than presenting it as an observed result.
Retesting should record whether the original issue remains, which version was checked, and any limitations. Closing one finding doesn’t establish that every related feature is secure.
The report’s value is in those specifics. OWASP references help organise the work, but they do not confer provider certification or guarantee that every vulnerability will be found. Likewise, checking selected ASVS requirements should not be described as full verification of an ASVS level.
References OWASP Top 10:2025 OWASP WSTG v4.2 OWASP ASVS OWASP API Security Top 10:2023 Reviewed 10 November 2026. The invoice portal is a worked example.
title: What does an OWASP-based penetration test actually cover?

contents:
An AI tool reads an API specification and suggests a possible access-control problem. That might be a useful lead. Before it belongs in a penetration test report, someone needs to establish whether the endpoint exists in the tested version, whether the suspected behaviour is reachable, and what actually happens when it is tested.
That gap between a suggestion and a finding is where much of the work remains.
Give the tool a specific job There are sensible uses for AI during an assessment: organising notes, suggesting questions from a sanitised design document, grouping similar observations, or improving a report’s wording. The tester should be able to explain which of those jobs the tool performed.
For example, a model might group several access-control observations as duplicates. Before removing any of them, check the affected roles and endpoints. Two responses that look similar may expose different resources or require different fixes.
Report editing needs the same care. A smoother sentence can quietly strengthen a claim. “This response suggests that another user’s record may be accessible” must not become “An attacker can access all customer records” unless the evidence establishes that impact.
Agree the boundaries before active testing When a tool can send requests or invoke other tools, define what it is allowed to do. The engagement still needs named assets, permitted techniques, a testing window, and a way to stop activity.
A useful planning question is what happens if the tool discovers a new hostname. Is it inside the authorised scope? Who checks? A model’s decision that the host looks relevant is not permission to test it.
The same applies to instructions encountered during testing. A response body or a retrieved document can contain text aimed at the testing agent. That material is part of the system being examined; it cannot authorise a new action or change the engagement rules.
Know where the evidence goes Before using a model with client material, establish which provider receives the input, what is retained, and who can access it. Source code, request captures, and screenshots may include credentials or personal data even when they look like ordinary debugging material.
Use synthetic examples or remove unnecessary fields where possible. Sanitisation needs checking too: removing a token from the request doesn’t help if the same token remains in a response, a screenshot, or an attached log.
A buyer should be able to ask how AI is used and receive a concrete answer. “We use AI to make testing faster” doesn’t explain the data handling or the controls around active tests.
What should survive into the report? The report needs the evidence that supports a finding: the affected asset, prerequisites, relevant requests and responses, observed impact, and a fix the engineering team can work with. It should also state what could not be verified.
The number of generated test cases is a poor substitute for that record. Ten well-chosen tests of a sensitive workflow may answer a question that hundreds of generic requests never reach.
Human validation should mean someone has checked the technical evidence and accepted responsibility for the finding. It should be possible to explain why the finding is valid without referring to the model’s confidence or wording.
AI use and accreditation CREST’s July 2026 announcement introduced responsible-AI organisational requirements and an AI-enabled penetration testing annex. It also distinguishes AI used within a testing service from security testing of AI systems themselves.
When assessing a provider, verify its current accreditation and the services covered. An application for accreditation or the use of an AI product doesn’t establish that status. The questions in this article are intended to help evaluate a testing process; Actiotech is not claiming AI accreditation here.
References CREST AI accreditation announcement CREST accreditation standards OWASP AI/LLM application security testing Reviewed 10 November 2026.
title: Using AI during a penetration test

contents:
Imagine an assistant that summarises a Jira project and offers to create follow-up tasks. In a demo, it reads the issues, writes a helpful summary, and creates a task when asked. Everything appears to work.
Now give the same assistant to someone who can see only part of that project. Which issues enter the summary? Does the assistant’s cached answer contain information the person cannot read? If it creates a task, whose permissions does it use?
These questions are worth answering before spending the whole test session on hostile prompts.
Trace one summary request Start at retrieval. Identify the user asking the question and the identity used to fetch issues or documents. Atlassian’s cloud app security requirements apply to the app’s authentication and authorisation decisions; adding a model doesn’t move those decisions into the prompt.
Check the retrieved records before they reach the model. If a restricted issue is included, telling the assistant not to disclose confidential information leaves the access-control problem in place.
Then follow the answer into caches, logs, exports, and conversation history. A permission check at retrieval time won’t necessarily protect a summary that is later served from a shared cache.
Set up a test you can observe Use synthetic issues and documents in an authorised test environment. Create two roles with different access and, where the app supports it, two separate tenant installations. Put a distinctive, harmless marker in each restricted record.
Ask for a summary as the less-privileged user. Inspect the retrieval results, the material sent to the model, the generated answer, and any stored copy. The marker helps establish whether restricted content travelled further than it should have.
Next, remove a permission and repeat the request. Check the existing conversation as well as a fresh one. Cached summaries and older retrieval indexes deserve attention because they can preserve access after the underlying permission has changed.
Separate reading from acting An assistant that proposes a task has different privileges from one that creates it. Decide which behaviour the product needs and expose only the corresponding tool operations.
The tool handler should check the target resource, the caller’s permission, and the submitted arguments. A prompt instruction such as “only change issues the user can edit” is not an authorisation check.
For a consequential action, show the user the proposed target and content before confirmation. If the assistant changes either after approval, that approval no longer describes the action being taken. This is especially relevant when a conversation moves between several projects or issues.
Then test untrusted content The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications includes prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, improper output handling, and excessive agency. Those categories point to different parts of this example.
Place a benign instruction in a test issue description and check whether it redirects the assistant away from the user’s task. Watch the tool calls and resulting changes, not only the chat reply. An assistant could refuse an instruction in its response after a tool has already acted on it.
Also inspect how generated content is rendered. Model output that becomes HTML, a link, or a tool argument needs handling appropriate to that destination. Test failures and repeated calls with bounded budgets so the test itself doesn’t create uncontrolled processing.
Keep the failure as a regression case For each issue, save the permission state, the relevant synthetic input, the requested action, and the observed result. Repeat the case after changes to retrieval, tool permissions, prompts, or the model. For variable behaviour, record how many attempts were made rather than describing one successful run as a general guarantee.
The OWASP testing guidance is useful when planning this wider assessment. The aim is to understand what the whole application can disclose or change, including the ordinary access-control defects an impressive AI demo can make easy to overlook.
References Atlassian cloud app security requirements OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications OWASP AI/LLM testing guidance Reviewed 10 November 2026. The assistant is a worked example.
title: Testing an AI assistant inside a Jira app
